briefings.title: Where AI helps UX research, and where not
briefings.dek: Teams must decide which research tasks to hand to AI and which to keep with human researchers.
briefings.scenario: A research group at a large retailer has thousands of open-ended survey comments nobody has time to read, and a leader asks whether synthetic users could replace some recruited sessions. The team needs to decide which of those requests is reasonable and which could mislead product decisions.

positions.label: Delegate comment coding
positions.summary: Sorting open-ended survey comments into themes is the clearest assistant-level job for AI. One source reports AI now matches human researchers at it, and another has tracked the idea for three years as a promising use.

positions.label: Hold back on judgment work
positions.summary: Finding usability problems has produced mixed results so far. Synthetic users are contested: they may suit rough, low-stakes artifacts or early exploration, but one source says they give feedback that is too positive, and another urges very limited use for a human-centered discipline.

briefings.context: Interest in AI for research has moved from whether it can replace researchers to which tasks it can take on. The sources split the work into assistant-level tasks, such as coding comments, and analyst-level tasks, such as spotting usability problems or standing in for participants. Researchers are also divided on whether synthetic users are acceptable at all.

steps.label: Pilot comment coding
steps.text: Run AI coding on a past survey where human-coded themes already exist, and compare the two before relying on it.

steps.label: Limit synthetic users
steps.text: Use them only for early exploration or rough artifacts, and treat their feedback as likely too favorable.

steps.label: Keep humans on findings
steps.text: Have researchers decide which usability problems are real, and use AI output only as a second set of observations to check against theirs.

briefings.caveat: The excerpts are short and give no study methods or error rates, so they don't show how well AI performs across different products, participants, or datasets.

briefings.title: Naming conventions or an agent for system upkeep
briefings.dek: Teams must decide whether design system coherence comes mainly from human-readable naming structures or from an agent that takes over repetitive maintenance.
briefings.scenario: A design system team at a large retailer has a component library that has drifted, with inconsistent names and product designs that stray from approved patterns. They have to choose between writing and enforcing a naming guide, or piloting an agent to handle library upkeep and keep designs aligned.

positions.label: Name things deliberately
positions.summary: The Smashing guide treats naming of UI components as a craft problem and offers conventions, structures, and reference resources. The implied route to coherence is shared vocabulary that people apply by hand.

positions.label: Automate the repetitive upkeep
positions.summary: Figma's post presents its agent as a way to take on routine work in a design system, including library maintenance and helping designs follow the system. The implied route to coherence is offloading chores rather than relying on people to do them.

briefings.context: Design systems tend to lose consistency as they grow, through naming drift, outdated components, and designs that depart from the library. The two articles address different layers of that problem: how components are labeled and structured, and who carries out the ongoing maintenance. One is a general guide to practice, the other a vendor's description of its own tool.

steps.label: Audit current drift
steps.text: List where your system is actually inconsistent, separating naming problems from maintenance backlog and from designs that ignore the library.

steps.label: Set naming first
steps.text: Agree on a convention and structure for components so that any person or tool working on the library has a clear pattern to follow.

steps.label: Pilot on chores
steps.text: Try the agent on one bounded, repetitive task and have a person review the results before widening its scope.

briefings.caveat: The excerpts don't show how well the agent performs or whether it depends on good naming, so they can't say whether the two approaches compete or complement each other.

briefings.title: Delegating design work to agents: where limits appear
briefings.dek: Teams must decide which design tasks to give an AI agent now, and how to check that it holds up on large, interconnected projects.
briefings.scenario: A design org at a large enterprise software company is reworking a platform with hundreds of linked screens. Leadership wants an agent to update components, collect critique feedback and draft specs, but nobody knows whether it will cope with the full scope.

positions.label: Hand off bounded chores
positions.summary: Figma's own workflow pieces describe the designer working on the core problem while the agent takes library updates, critique feedback and a first-draft spec. They also say deciding what to delegate is a skill in itself. A separate piece casts a fast, token-efficient model as a capable entry-level helper.

positions.label: Scale exposes the gaps
positions.summary: One practitioner tried AI-assisted interface generation ahead of designing 800+ interconnected enterprise screens. The test ran into trouble with visual quality and, by the author's account, never got to the hard part of the project.

briefings.context: Figma's agent is now generally available, and its blog is showcasing product teams that use it for speed and craft. Independent writers are testing similar AI tooling against less tidy conditions. The vendor examples centre on well-scoped tasks, while the critical account involves a large system with many dependencies.

steps.label: Pilot small tasks
steps.text: Start with contained work such as library updates, critique summaries and first-draft specs, and have a designer review every output.

steps.label: Keep judgment human
steps.text: Leave the framing of the problem and the decisions about how screens connect with the designers who own the project.

steps.label: Stress-test early
steps.text: Run the agent against a realistic slice of your most interconnected flows before committing it to the whole program.

briefings.caveat: These are short excerpts, the Figma pieces come from the vendor, and none of them gives measured error rates or a direct comparison of agent output with human work on a large project.

briefings.title: Automate less, and design oversight people can sustain
briefings.dek: Teams must decide how much work to hand to AI and whether asking people to supervise it is a workable safeguard.
briefings.scenario: A product team at a large insurer plans to let an AI system process most claims and route a few flagged cases to adjusters for approval. Leadership calls this human-in-the-loop, but the team suspects reviewers will stop looking closely once most flags turn out to be fine.

positions.label: Design for vigilance limits
positions.summary: Human attention fails in two ways: it fades during long monitoring, and it fades again across repeated occasional approval requests. Oversight only holds up if the watching shifts are short and the questions put to people are rare and meaningful.

positions.label: Automate with intention
positions.summary: Many organizations chase full automation without checking whether they are ready or whether customers benefit. The argument is to set a deliberate direction and sequence automation, drawing on human factors and systems thinking, rather than treating AI as a break from earlier automation.

briefings.context: Human factors research on monitoring and automation predates current AI, and these pieces apply it to AI products. Two of the three are from the same author, so the vigilance argument is overrepresented. The third is a book promotion that frames automation as a strategy problem.

steps.label: Audit oversight points
steps.text: List every place a person is expected to watch or approve AI output, and estimate how often each one actually requires a real judgment.

steps.label: Shorten and ration
steps.text: Cap continuous monitoring stretches and cut approval prompts to the cases that truly need a person, so each question stays meaningful.

steps.label: Sequence automation
steps.text: Tie each step toward more automation to evidence of readiness and customer value, rather than to a fully automated end state.

briefings.caveat: The excerpts give no evidence on how to calibrate automation levels in specific domains, and the figures cited come from one author's summary of monitoring research.
